answer: Second-order proximity, as used in network embedding (e.g., LINE, Tang et al. 2015), is defined over the neighborhood structure of vertices rather than their direct links. Two vertices u and v have high second-order proximity when their neighborhood network structures are similar: it compares the sets of vertices each one is connected to (their neighbor/context vectors), i.e., whether u and v share many of the same neighbors or have similar distributions over their out-neighbors. Formally, if p_u = (w_{u,1}, ..., w_{u,|V|}) is the vector of u's weights to all vertices (its first-order connections as the 'context' view), then second-order proximity between u and v is measured by the similarity of p_u and p_v (e.g., via conditional probabilities p2(v_j|v_i) = w_{ij}/sum_k w_{ik} and minimizing KL divergence between these distributions). Thus, two vertices are second-order similar if they have shared neighbors and similar neighborhood structure, even when they are not directly linked to each other.
